name: Barbell Bench Press
cues: Tuck elbows to ~45-60 degrees, not flared to 90
Set the scapulae down and back before you unrack
Touch the lower sternum, drive the bar back over the shoulder
notes: Nippard ranks this A-tier rather than S-tier: great for load and progression, but the bar stops at the ribcage so the chest never reaches a full stretch. Cavaliere flags flat barbell benching as a common source of anterior shoulder pain.

name: Incline Barbell Bench Press
cues: Set the bench to ~30 degrees, not 45
Bar path to the upper sternum/clavicle
Keep the ribcage proud, don't let it flatten out
notes: ~30 degrees biases the clavicular head without turning the lift into a shoulder press. Steeper inclines shift work to the front delts.

name: Decline Barbell Bench Press
cues: Short range, heavy load - control the eccentric
Keep the bar over the lower chest
Don't bounce off the ribcage
notes: Lowest-priority chest press. Sternal-head emphasis is real but small, and setup friction is high.

name: Dumbbell Bench Press
cues: Let the dumbbells travel past the ribcage for a deep stretch
Slight arc in, don't clash them at the top
Neutral-to-45 degree grip if the shoulder is cranky
notes: Nippard's stated reason for rating dumbbells above the barbell for hypertrophy: the hands can move past the torso, so the pec reaches a longer muscle length. Cavaliere prefers dumbbells for shoulder-friendly pressing.

name: Incline Dumbbell Press
cues: 30 degree bench, dumbbells travel toward the collarbones
Stretch deep at the bottom without shrugging
Stop just short of lockout to keep tension
notes: Best single upper-chest builder in the library on a stretch + SFR basis.

name: Machine Chest Press
cues: Set the handle height at mid-chest
Let the handles come back until you feel the pec stretch
Push away from your body, not just up
notes: Nippard's top-ranked chest exercise for hypertrophy. Stabilization is offloaded, so nearly all the fatigue lands on the chest - excellent late-mesocycle option and safe to take near failure.

name: Incline Machine Press
cues: Handles at upper-chest height
Deep stretch, controlled 2-second eccentric
Keep the back flat against the pad
notes: Incline pressing with stabilisation offloaded to the machine. Good late-mesocycle upper-chest volume once free-weight incline work is already costing you.

name: Smith Machine Incline Press
cues: Position the bench so the bar path lands on the upper chest
Use the safeties - you can train close to failure alone
Controlled eccentric, no bounce
notes: Fixed bar path is a feature here: lets you push closer to failure solo.

name: Push-Up
cues: Hands slightly wider than shoulders, elbows ~45 degrees
Squeeze glutes and brace - the body moves as one plank
Protract the shoulder blades at the top
notes: Cavaliere considers the push-up a foundational movement most lifters abandon too early. The top-end protraction is serratus work you don't get from bench pressing.

name: Incline Push-Up
cues: Higher hands = easier; lower the surface as you progress
Same rigid plank as a floor push-up
Full range: chest to the surface
notes: Primary regression for anyone who can't do clean floor push-ups.

name: Deficit Push-Up
cues: Hands on handles or dumbbells so the chest can drop below them
Own the bottom stretch for a full second
Don't let the low back sag
notes: Adds the stretch the standard push-up lacks.

name: Weighted Push-Up
cues: Plate on the upper back or a band across the shoulder blades
Brace hard - the load wants to break the plank
Full protraction at the top
notes: Restores progressive overload to the push-up while keeping its top-end scapular protraction. Band resistance matches the strength curve better than a plate does.

name: Chest Dip
cues: Lean the torso forward ~30 degrees to bias the chest
Descend until the upper arm is roughly parallel
Stop if you feel a pinch at the front of the shoulder
notes: High joint stress at the bottom. Cavaliere-style caution: this is a common anterior shoulder aggravator; limit depth before you limit load.

name: Assisted Dip
cues: Use the least assistance that lets you control the bottom
Keep the shoulders down, away from the ears
Stop above any pinch point
notes: Bridge to unassisted dips. Reduce the assistance rather than chasing reps once you clear 12.

name: Weighted Dip
cues: Add load only once bodyweight dips are effortless for 12+
Controlled eccentric - this is where shoulders get hurt
Torso forward for chest, upright for triceps
notes: Strong chest/triceps compound, but the loaded bottom position is where shoulders get hurt. Earn it with clean bodyweight reps before adding a belt.

name: Seated Cable Fly
cues: Slight elbow bend, hold it fixed the whole set
Think 'hug a barrel' - hands meet in front of the sternum
Let the arms travel behind the torso for a full stretch
notes: Nippard ranks this at or near the top for chest: constant tension plus loaded stretch, minimal fatigue cost.

name: Cable Fly (Mid)
cues: Split stance, torso leaned slightly forward
Fixed elbow angle - this is a fly, not a press
Cross the hands slightly at the finish
notes: Standing crossover at mid-pulley height. Constant tension across the whole arc and a trivial fatigue cost, so it stacks well late in a mesocycle.

name: Low-to-High Cable Fly
cues: Pulleys at the bottom, hands finish at chin height
Keep the elbow angle locked
Squeeze for a beat at the top
notes: Upper-chest bias.

name: High-to-Low Cable Fly
cues: Pulleys high, hands finish at the hips
Lean in slightly, chest tall
Don't turn it into a pushdown
notes: Lower/sternal chest bias.

name: Pec Deck
cues: Set the seat so the handles sit at chest height
Back flat against the pad throughout
Pause a beat in the stretched position
notes: Easiest chest isolation to take safely to failure.

name: Dumbbell Fly
cues: Soft, fixed elbow bend
Stop the descent at a stretch you control
Resistance disappears at the top - don't chase it
notes: Ranked below cable and machine flies: the resistance profile is worst exactly where the chest is strongest, and the stretch position is the most shoulder-vulnerable.

name: Svend Press
cues: Squeeze two plates together at chest height
Press straight out, keep squeezing
Slow return
notes: Included for completeness only - Nippard ranks the plate press dead last for chest. Very low tension, near-zero progression path. Do not program by default.

name: Barbell Overhead Press
cues: Squeeze glutes and abs - no lumbar layback
Move the head back, then through, as the bar passes
Finish with the bar over the mid-foot, biceps by the ears
notes: Best overhead strength builder. Never press behind the neck - Cavaliere lists it among the highest-risk shoulder positions.

name: Seated Dumbbell Shoulder Press
cues: Start with the dumbbells at ear height, elbows slightly forward
Let the shoulder blades rotate naturally - don't lock them down
Press up and slightly in
notes: Cavaliere's preferred overhead press: independent arms let the scapula move through its natural rhythm instead of being forced into a fixed bar path.

name: Standing Dumbbell Shoulder Press
cues: Ribs down, glutes tight
No leg drive - keep it strict
Full lockout overhead
notes: More core demand, less load. Cavaliere's 'train like an athlete' preference for standing over seated where practical.

name: Machine Shoulder Press
cues: Handles start at ear height
Back flat on the pad
Stop just short of full lockout
notes: Safest way to take overhead pressing near failure.

name: Arnold Press
cues: Start palms-in at the chest, rotate as you press
Keep the rotation smooth, not jerky
Lighter load than a standard press
notes: The rotation under load is a shoulder-irritation risk for some. Marginal benefit over a standard DB press.

name: Landmine Press
cues: Press up and forward along the bar's arc
Let the shoulder blade travel with the arm
Stay tall - no side bend
notes: Cavaliere's go-to press for anyone whose shoulder dislikes true vertical pressing. The arc sits in the scapular plane.

name: Pike Push-Up
cues: Hips high, body in an inverted V
Lower the crown of the head toward the floor
Elbows track slightly forward
notes: Bodyweight bridge toward vertical pressing. Elevate the feet to increase the overhead component.

name: Handstand Push-Up
cues: Heels lightly on the wall, body stacked
Lower under control - no crashing
Full lockout, shoulders shrugged at the top
notes: High skill, high joint stress. Athletic-quality movement, mediocre hypertrophy tool.

name: Dumbbell Front Raise
cues: Raise to eye level, no higher
Thumbs slightly up
No torso swing
notes: Front delt MEV is 0 for most lifters who press. Program only for a specific weak point.

name: Cable Front Raise
cues: Cable from behind for tension in the stretch
Raise to eye level
Fixed elbow angle
notes: Front delt MEV is 0 for most people who press at all. Program this only to address a demonstrated weak point.

name: Dumbbell Lateral Raise
cues: Lead with the elbows, not the hands
Stop at shoulder height - higher is traps
Slow the eccentric, don't drop
notes: Highest-MRV shoulder muscle; tolerates a lot of weekly volume. Cavaliere's fix for people who reach for upright rows.

name: Cable Lateral Raise
cues: Cable running behind the body, across the front
Tension is highest at the bottom - that's the point
Elbow leads, wrist neutral
notes: Better resistance profile than dumbbells: loaded in the stretched position where dumbbells give you nothing.

name: Machine Lateral Raise
cues: Pads on the upper arm, not the forearm
Drive with the elbow
Control all the way down
notes: Easiest side-delt movement to take to failure safely - useful in the final mesocycle weeks.

name: Lean-Away Lateral Raise
cues: Hold an upright, lean the torso away
Lets the delt work through a longer range
Same elbow-leads cue
notes: Increases the loaded range compared to a standing bilateral raise.

name: Lu Raise
cues: Raise all the way overhead, palms up at the top
Very light load
Keep the motion continuous
notes: Full overhead range recruits traps heavily; treat as a shoulder/trap combo, not a pure side-delt movement.

name: Cable Y-Raise
cues: Finish in a wide Y overhead, thumbs up
Light load, full scapular upward rotation
No shrugging into the ears
notes: Cavaliere programs Y-pattern work for lower-trap and scapular upward rotation - direct antidote to a push-heavy week.

name: Upright Row
cues: Wide grip only - narrow grips force internal rotation
Stop at chest height, never higher
If there is any pinch, stop and substitute
notes: Highest-risk shoulder movement in the library. Internal rotation plus elevation is the classic impingement position. Cavaliere would substitute lateral raises and face pulls. Do not auto-program; keep it available for users who specifically want it.

name: Face Pull
cues: Rope at eye height, pull to the forehead
Finish with the thumbs back and elbows high
External rotation at the end - separate the rope ends
notes: Cavaliere's signature prescription: do these after EVERY workout, push or pull or legs. Hits rear delts, rotator cuff external rotators, and scapular retractors in one movement. Never take to failure - 2-3 sets at RIR 3-4.

name: Band Pull-Apart
cues: Arms straight, pull the band to the chest
Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the end
Slow return, don't let it snap back
notes: Zero-equipment warm-up staple. Good pre-press activation for the upper back.

name: Reverse Pec Deck
cues: Chest against the pad, slight elbow bend
Drive the elbows back and out, not down
Pause a beat at full retraction
notes: Best pure rear-delt isolation on SFR grounds. Very high MRV muscle - can be trained 3-4x/week.

name: Dumbbell Reverse Fly
cues: Hinge to ~45 degrees, flat back
Pinkies slightly up at the top
Light load - momentum kills this one
notes: Resistance profile is poor at the stretch. Cable or machine versions are better.

name: Cable Reverse Fly
cues: Cross the cables, pull wide and back
Constant tension through the whole arc
Chest up, don't round forward
notes: Constant-tension rear delt work. Rear delts recover quickly and tolerate 3-4 sessions per week.

name: Chest-Supported Rear Delt Row
cues: Incline bench, row with elbows high and wide
Pull toward the upper chest line, not the hips
Squeeze the shoulder blades at the top
notes: Rear delts plus upper back in one movement - efficient for tight schedules.

name: Prone Incline Y-Raise
cues: Face down on an incline, arms form a Y overhead
Thumbs up, very light dumbbells
Lead with the lower traps, not the upper
notes: Lower-trap specific. Cavaliere's fix for the scapular dyskinesis that comes with heavy pressing volume.

name: Prone W-Raise
cues: Elbows bent, arms form a W
Rotate the thumbs back and up
Tiny weights - 2-5 kg is plenty
notes: Cavaliere prehab staple for the external rotators and mid/lower traps.

name: Scapular Pull-Up
cues: Arms stay straight - only the shoulder blades move
Pull the chest up an inch by depressing the scapulae
Full relaxed hang at the bottom
notes: Teaches scapular depression before pull-ups. Cavaliere programs this as both prehab and pull-up prerequisite.

name: Scapular Push-Up
cues: Arms locked straight - only the shoulder blades move
Push the floor away to protract fully
Slow, controlled, no sagging hips
notes: Serratus anterior. Cavaliere's answer to winged scapulae and poor overhead mechanics.

name: Dead Hang
cues: Relax into the hang, let the shoulders rise
Breathe
Time in seconds, not reps
notes: Grip endurance plus shoulder decompression. Rep range here is SECONDS, not reps - the UI must handle time-based prescriptions.

name: Pull-Up
cues: Start from a full dead hang, shoulder blades relaxed
Pull the elbows down and back toward the ribs
Chest to the bar, controlled descent
notes: Best bodyweight back builder. Cavaliere insists on full dead-hang range; partial-range pull-ups are the most common technique error.

name: Chin-Up
cues: Supinated, shoulder-width grip
Drive the elbows down toward the hips
Full extension at the bottom
notes: More biceps than the pull-up; counts as 1.0 lats plus 1.0 biceps in the set-counting model.

name: Neutral-Grip Pull-Up
cues: Palms facing each other
Elbows drive straight down
Full range top and bottom
notes: Cavaliere's default pull-up variation for anyone with elbow or shoulder sensitivity - the neutral grip is the least stressful position for both joints.

name: Assisted Pull-Up
cues: Use the least assistance you can control
Same full-range standard as an unassisted pull-up
Don't bounce off the bottom
notes: Lets you train the full dead-hang range before you can do it unloaded. Note that band assistance helps most at the bottom and least at the top, which is where most people actually fail — the machine is more honest.

name: Eccentric-Only Pull-Up
cues: Jump or step to the top position
Lower over 5 seconds, fighting the whole way
Reset - don't rush between reps
notes: Fastest route from assisted to unassisted pull-ups. Expect high soreness - cap at 2-3 sets.

name: Weighted Pull-Up
cues: Only add load once 12 clean bodyweight reps are easy
Keep the full dead-hang standard
Control the descent - this is where the elbows complain
notes: Add load only once 12 clean bodyweight reps are easy. The eccentric is where elbows start complaining, so control it.

name: Lat Pulldown
cues: Grip just outside shoulder width - ultra-wide is not better
Let the shoulder blades rise at the top for a full stretch
Pull to the upper chest, elbows down and back
notes: Highest-SFR lat builder. Easy to load precisely and take near failure. Ultra-wide grips shorten the range for no benefit - a common technique error Nippard calls out.

name: Neutral-Grip Lat Pulldown
cues: V-handle or neutral bar
Lean back ~15 degrees, chest to the handle
Full stretch overhead each rep
notes: Joint-friendliest pulldown variation.

name: Kneeling Cable Pulldown
cues: Kneel far enough back that the cable line is diagonal
Pull to the sternum, ribs down
Let the arms travel fully overhead at the top
notes: Nippard favourite: the diagonal cable line matches lat fibre orientation better than a vertical pulldown.

name: Straight-Arm Pulldown
cues: Arms nearly straight, slight fixed elbow bend
Hinge slightly at the hips, chest down
Pull the bar to the thighs using the lats, not the triceps
notes: Isolates the lat's shoulder-extension function without any elbow flexion - useful when biceps are the limiting factor.

name: Dumbbell Pullover
cues: Lie across or along a bench, dumbbell over the chest
Lower behind the head until you feel the lat stretch
Keep the elbows only slightly bent
notes: Loaded stretch for the lats. Shoulder-extension end range can be uncomfortable - regress to straight-arm pulldowns if so.

name: Machine Pullover
cues: Elbows on the pads, drive down and back
Full overhead stretch each rep
Torso stays still
notes: Best-in-class lat stretch if your gym has one.

name: Barbell Row
cues: Hinge to ~45 degrees, flat back, braced
Row to the lower ribs, elbows ~45 degrees from the torso
No jerking - the torso angle doesn't change
notes: High systemic and lower-back cost. Great strength builder, mediocre SFR for pure hypertrophy. Program early in the session, not late in the mesocycle.

name: Pendlay Row
cues: Torso parallel to the floor, bar resets on the floor each rep
Explosive concentric to the lower chest
Brace hard before every rep
notes: Highest lower-back cost in the row family. Strength-focused blocks only.

name: Dumbbell Row
cues: Let the shoulder blade travel forward at the bottom for a full stretch
Row to the hip, elbow close to the body
Don't rotate the torso to cheat the last reps
notes: Cavaliere likes the unilateral loading for addressing side-to-side asymmetry.

name: Chest-Supported Row
cues: Chest stays on the pad the entire set
Row to the lower ribs, squeeze at the top
Full stretch at the bottom - let the arms hang
notes: Best SFR row: zero lower-back cost, so you can add volume freely. Cavaliere's substitution for anyone with low-back issues from bent-over rowing.

name: Seal Row
cues: Lie face-down on a high bench, bar hangs freely
Pull to the lower ribs, pause at the top
Strict - no body English is even possible
notes: The most honest row: momentum is mechanically impossible.

name: T-Bar Row
cues: Hinge, flat back, chest over the bar
Pull to the sternum
Control the stretch at the bottom
notes: Chest-supported versions remove the lower-back cost; the free version is a genuine strength lift with real spinal loading. Pick based on what else is in the week.

name: Seated Cable Row
cues: Let the shoulder blades protract fully at the front
Pull to the navel, elbows past the torso
Torso stays roughly upright - no rocking
notes: Workhorse back movement. Very high SFR, easy load progression.

name: Wide-Grip Seated Cable Row
cues: Wide bar, elbows flare to ~90 degrees
Pull to the upper chest
Retract hard at the finish
notes: Upper back and rear delt bias vs. the standard row's lat bias.

name: Machine Row
cues: Chest against the pad
Full stretch, full squeeze
Drive the elbows back, don't yank with the hands
notes: High-SFR horizontal pull that is safe to take near failure, which makes it a good final-week row when the barbell version has become expensive.

name: Single-Arm Cable Row
cues: Let the shoulder reach forward at the front
Pull to the hip, allow slight torso rotation
Squeeze, then control the return
notes: Unilateral loading plus a longer range than a bilateral row.

name: Meadows Row
cues: Stand perpendicular to the bar, staggered stance
Row the sleeve up and back
Big stretch at the bottom
notes: The landmine angle gives a long stretch at the bottom and a strong contraction at the top. Unilateral, so it also exposes side-to-side asymmetry.

name: Inverted Row
cues: Body rigid from heels to head
Pull the chest to the bar
Lower the bar or elevate the feet to make it harder
notes: Cavaliere staple: infinitely scalable horizontal pull with zero spinal loading. Best first horizontal pull for beginners.

name: Barbell Shrug
cues: Straight up and down - no rolling the shoulders
Pause a beat at the top
Full stretch at the bottom, let the traps lengthen
notes: Shoulder rolling adds nothing and puts the joint in a bad spot at the back of the arc.

name: Dumbbell Shrug
cues: Arms hang straight, shrug to the ears
Hold the top for one second
Slow lower
notes: Simplest way to load the traps. Grip usually fails first — use straps once the traps outpace the hands.

name: Trap Bar Shrug
cues: Neutral grip, load stays at the sides
Vertical shrug, one-second hold
Don't lean back
notes: Best loading position for the traps - the weight is in line with the body.

name: Cable Shrug
cues: Constant tension top to bottom
Pause and squeeze at the top
Let the traps stretch fully at the bottom
notes: Constant tension top to bottom, unlike free weights where the bottom of the shrug unloads almost completely.

name: Farmer's Carry
cues: Tall posture, ribs down, shoulders packed
Short, quick steps
Prescribed in seconds or metres, not reps
notes: Cavaliere 'train like an athlete' staple: grip, core, postural endurance, and conditioning in one. Time- or distance-based, not rep-based.

name: Suitcase Carry
cues: Resist the side bend - stay perfectly upright
Don't let the loaded shoulder drop
Time-based, both sides equally
notes: Anti-lateral-flexion core work disguised as a carry.

name: Plate Pinch Carry
cues: Pinch two plates smooth-side out
Fingers straight, thumb opposing
Hold for time
notes: Pinch grip strength - the grip quality most lifters never train.

name: Barbell Curl
cues: Elbows pinned at the sides
Full extension at the bottom, no half reps
No hip swing - if the torso moves, drop the weight
notes: Fixed supinated grip on a straight bar is a common medial-elbow irritant. Cavaliere's substitution is the EZ bar or dumbbells.

name: EZ-Bar Curl
cues: Semi-supinated grip is easier on the wrists and elbows
Elbows stay at the sides
Full range top and bottom
notes: Default barbell curl for anyone with elbow sensitivity.

name: Dumbbell Curl
cues: Supinate as you curl - finish with the pinky high
Elbows stay under the shoulders
Control the lowering, don't drop
notes: Baseline biceps movement. Supination under load is part of what the biceps does, so let the hand rotate rather than fixing it.

name: Incline Dumbbell Curl
cues: Bench at ~45-60 degrees, arms hang behind the torso
Let the biceps fully stretch at the bottom
Keep the upper arm still
notes: Loads the long head at its longest length. Nippard's top biceps pick on stretch grounds.

name: Bayesian Cable Curl
cues: Step forward so the arm hangs behind the torso
Constant tension, especially in the stretch
Elbow stays fixed in space
notes: Cable equivalent of the incline curl, with a better resistance curve.

name: Cable Curl
cues: Constant tension throughout
Elbows at the sides
Squeeze at the top, resist on the way down
notes: Constant tension through the full range and generally easier on the elbows than a straight bar.

name: Preacher Curl
cues: Armpits into the top of the pad
Do not fully lock out under heavy load - the bottom is vulnerable
Controlled eccentric
notes: Strong short-head emphasis. Full extension under heavy load is a known biceps tendon/distal tear position - keep a few degrees of bend at the bottom.

name: Spider Curl
cues: Chest on an incline bench, arms hang vertically
Curl without swinging the upper arm
Peak contraction squeeze
notes: Short-head bias, strict by construction.

name: Hammer Curl
cues: Palms face each other throughout
Elbows pinned
Full extension at the bottom
notes: Brachialis and brachioradialis. Cavaliere's preferred curl for elbow-sensitive lifters.

name: Cross-Body Hammer Curl
cues: Curl across the body toward the opposite pec
Neutral grip the whole way
No shoulder shrug
notes: Brachialis emphasis with a slightly longer working range than a standard hammer curl.

name: Reverse Curl
cues: Overhand grip, wrists neutral and firm
Lighter than you think
Full range, no wrist flexion
notes: Brachioradialis and wrist extensors. Cavaliere programs this specifically as prehab against lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow).

name: Concentration Curl
cues: Elbow braced against the inner thigh
Full extension, full supination
No body English at all
notes: Highest measured biceps EMG of the common curls. Strict by design.

name: Close-Grip Bench Press
cues: Grip just inside shoulder width - not hands-together
Tuck elbows to ~30 degrees
Bar touches the lower sternum
notes: Too narrow a grip is a wrist and elbow irritant for no extra triceps recruitment.

name: Triceps Dip
cues: Torso vertical, elbows tracking straight back
Descend to upper arm parallel, no deeper
Lock out at the top
notes: Upright torso shifts emphasis from chest to triceps. High shoulder stress at depth.

name: Bench Dip
cues: Hands on the bench behind you, elbows back not out
Shallow range only
Stop immediately if the front of the shoulder complains
notes: Poor shoulder position (extension plus internal rotation). Included because it is common; prefer pushdowns or a real dip.

name: Overhead Cable Triceps Extension
cues: Face away from the stack, elbows beside the ears
Let the elbows travel forward for a deep long-head stretch
Elbows stay pointed forward, not flared
notes: Best long-head triceps builder - the only common triceps movement that loads the muscle at a long length. Nippard's top pick.

name: Dumbbell Overhead Triceps Extension
cues: One dumbbell in both hands, or one per arm
Elbows close, deep stretch behind the head
Don't let the elbows drift wide
notes: Long-head triceps work when no cable is available. The overhead stretch is the entire point — don't shorten it to move more weight.

name: EZ-Bar Skullcrusher
cues: Lower to the forehead or just behind the head
Elbows stay pointed at the ceiling, not flaring
Slight shoulder angle back keeps tension on the long head
notes: Classic elbow aggravator - Cavaliere's #1 movement to substitute for anyone with medial elbow pain. Use the EZ bar, never a straight bar, and keep it out of the last mesocycle week.

name: JM Press
cues: Halfway between a close-grip bench and a skullcrusher
Lower toward the chin with elbows tucked
Heavy elbow stress - build slowly
notes: Powerful triceps builder, high elbow cost. Advanced only.

name: Rope Triceps Pushdown
cues: Elbows pinned to the ribs
Separate the rope ends at the bottom
Don't lean over the bar and turn it into a press
notes: Highest-SFR triceps movement and the safest to take to failure. Cavaliere's default substitution for elbow-irritating extensions.

name: Straight-Bar Triceps Pushdown
cues: Elbows at the sides, wrists neutral
Full lockout, controlled return
Torso stays upright
notes: Straight-bar variant of the pushdown. Marginally more lateral-head bias than the rope; pick whichever your elbows and wrists prefer.

name: Triceps Kickback
cues: Upper arm parallel to the floor and fixed
Extend fully, squeeze at lockout
Very light load
notes: Peak contraction is in the shortened position where the triceps is weakest - poor resistance profile. Cable version is better than dumbbell.

name: Diamond Push-Up
cues: Hands form a triangle under the sternum
Elbows brush the ribs on the way down
Rigid plank throughout
notes: Wrist-intensive. Use push-up handles if the wrists complain.

name: Wrist Curl
cues: Forearms on a bench, wrists past the edge
Let the bar roll to the fingertips, then curl up
Full range, slow
notes: Direct forearm flexor work. Most lifters get enough from the grip demand of everything else — program it only when grip is a genuine limiter.

name: Reverse Wrist Curl
cues: Palms down, forearms braced
Very light load
Full extension, controlled lowering
notes: Cavaliere programs wrist extensor work as direct prehab for lateral elbow pain in lifters with heavy pulling volume.

name: Wrist Roller
cues: Arms out in front, roll up and down
One 'rep' = a full up-and-down cycle
Both directions - flexion and extension
notes: Rep range here means full roller cycles.

name: Barbell Back Squat
cues: Brace against the belt line before you descend
Knees track over the middle toes, don't cave
Descend to at least parallel, own the depth you use
notes: Highest systemic fatigue in the library - it eats into the recovery budget of everything else in the week. Program early in the session and early in the week. Israetel counts squat volume against quad MRV heavily.

name: Front Squat
cues: Elbows high throughout - the moment they drop, the bar does
Upright torso, deep knee bend
Full-depth only if the wrists and ankles allow it
notes: More quad-dominant and less lower-back-taxing than the back squat, but limited by front-rack mobility.

name: Safety Bar Squat
cues: Handles forward, upper back tight
The bar wants to tip you forward - fight it with the upper back
Same depth standard as a back squat
notes: Cavaliere's substitution for anyone whose shoulders can't tolerate the back-squat rack position. Also less shoulder-external-rotation demand.

name: Goblet Squat
cues: Hold the weight at the chest, elbows inside the knees
Sit straight down between the heels
Pause a beat at the bottom
notes: Best teaching squat. The counterweight makes an upright torso automatic.

name: Bodyweight Squat
cues: Feet shoulder-width, toes slightly out
Sit down and back, chest tall
Full depth if you own it
notes: Warm-up and true-beginner entry point.

name: Heels-Elevated Goblet Squat
cues: Heels on a 1-2 inch wedge or plates
Let the knees travel forward over the toes
Upright torso, full depth
notes: Heel elevation increases knee flexion and quad emphasis. Bridges conventional squatting and the knees-over-toes philosophy.

name: Hack Squat
cues: Feet low and close for maximum quad
Descend deep - the machine supports your back
Don't lock out hard at the top
notes: Top-tier quad hypertrophy tool: near-squat stimulus, far less systemic and spinal fatigue. High SFR.

name: Pendulum Squat
cues: Arced path keeps tension constant
Deep range, controlled tempo
Feet placement changes quad vs glute bias
notes: If available, arguably the best quad machine - excellent resistance curve, minimal spinal load.

name: Leg Press
cues: Feet mid-platform, shoulder width
Descend until the hips are about to round - not past
Never lock the knees out hard
notes: Very high SFR for quad volume. Cavaliere's substitution for anyone with back issues who still needs leg volume.

name: Smith Machine Squat
cues: Feet slightly forward of the bar
Use the safeties and train close to failure
Full depth
notes: The fixed bar path removes balance as a limiter, so you can push quads closer to failure training alone. Not a replacement for learning to squat free.

name: Belt Squat
cues: Load hangs from the hips - zero spinal compression
Full depth, upright torso
Hold the handles lightly for balance only
notes: Best option when spinal erectors are the limiting factor for leg volume.

name: Leg Extension
cues: Align the knee joint with the machine's pivot
Full lockout, one-second squeeze
Control the lowering - don't let the stack slam
notes: Only movement that trains the rectus femoris at the knee without hip flexion competing. End-range under heavy load can irritate the patellofemoral joint - regress the range before the load.

name: Sissy Squat
cues: Knees travel forward, hips stay extended
Lean back as the knees bend
Go only as deep as you can control
notes: Extreme knee flexion under bodyweight load. Ben Patrick uses it as a knee-resilience tool; build the range slowly and never rush it. ROM progression: measured as knee-flexion depth / lean-back angle you can control and return from; add range before adding load.

name: Reverse Nordic Curl
cues: Kneel tall, glutes squeezed, lean back from the knees
Only go as far as you can return from
Slow eccentric - 3 seconds minimum
notes: Loaded-stretch quad work with no equipment. Excellent knee-tendon conditioning; expect real soreness the first few sessions. ROM progression: measured as the backward lean angle from the knees you can return from unassisted.

name: Bulgarian Split Squat
cues: Rear foot on a bench, front shin free to travel
Torso upright for quads, leaned forward for glutes
Drive through the whole front foot
notes: High stimulus, high discomfort. Balance demand can limit the load before the muscle does - hold onto something if needed.

name: Split Squat
cues: Feet in a stable split stance, both feet flat
Descend straight down, back knee toward the floor
Front knee tracks over the middle toes
notes: Entry point for the Knees Over Toes split squat ladder.

name: ATG Split Squat
cues: Front foot elevated, let the knee travel well past the toes
Descend until the hamstring covers the calf
Back leg stays long and stretched - this is a hip flexor stretch too
notes: Ben Patrick's flagship movement. Progression standard: full bodyweight range with the hamstring covering the calf, pain-free, before loading. Published loaded benchmark is roughly 50% bodyweight for 10 reps. Progress the RANGE before the LOAD - always. ROM progression: measured as front-knee depth — advance until the hamstring covers the calf at full bodyweight, pain-free, before adding any load.

name: Patrick Step
cues: Stand on a low box, heel of the working leg hangs off
Reach the free leg back and down, keeping the working heel down
Small range at first - build it over weeks
notes: Ben Patrick's VMO/knee-resilience step. First rung of the knees-over-toes knee ladder after basic split squats. ROM progression: measured as how far the free heel descends toward the floor with the working heel down; add depth before adding load.

name: Poliquin Step-Up
cues: Toes on a raised wedge, step up onto a low box
Knee travels forward over the toes
Slow and controlled both directions
notes: Bridges the Patrick step and the ATG split squat in the knee ladder. ROM progression: measured as forefoot wedge height plus box height — increase knee-forward travel before adding load.

name: Step-Up
cues: Box height at or just above knee level
Drive entirely through the top foot - no push-off from the bottom
Lower under control, don't drop
notes: Cavaliere favourite for unilateral strength with minimal spinal load.

name: Walking Lunge
cues: Long stride for glutes, short stride for quads
Back knee lightly touches or nearly touches
Torso stays tall
notes: Very high soreness per set - the eccentric load is substantial. Count generously against MRV.

name: Reverse Lunge
cues: Step back, not forward - much kinder on the front knee
Front shin stays more vertical
Drive back to standing through the front heel
notes: Cavaliere's standard substitution for anyone with anterior knee pain from forward lunging.

name: Deficit Reverse Lunge
cues: Front foot on a 3-6 inch platform
Step back and down for extra hip flexion
Torso leans slightly forward for glute emphasis
notes: Extra range at the hip - strong glute stretch position.

name: Cossack Squat
cues: Shift the weight onto one bent leg, other leg straight
Keep the straight leg's heel down, toe up
Chest tall - resist folding forward
notes: Frontal-plane mobility and adductor strength through range. Both a KOT and an athletic-prep staple. ROM progression: measured as depth on the bent leg while the straight leg's heel stays flat on the floor.

name: Lateral Lunge
cues: Step wide to the side, sit back into that hip
Trailing leg stays straight
Push back to centre through the loaded heel
notes: Frontal-plane loading that most programs skip entirely. Builds adductor strength through range rather than just in a static hold.

name: Wall Sit
cues: Thighs parallel, back flat on the wall
Breathe through it
Prescribed in seconds
notes: Isometric quad work with negligible joint stress. Useful when knees are irritable and dynamic loading isn't tolerated. Time-based.

name: Conventional Deadlift
cues: Bar over mid-foot, shoulders slightly ahead of the bar
Take the slack out, then push the floor away
Lats engaged - keep the bar dragging up the legs
notes: Enormous systemic fatigue for modest hypertrophy return - Israetel's classic low-SFR example. Excellent strength lift, poor volume driver. Cap at 2-4 hard sets/week in a hypertrophy block.

name: Sumo Deadlift
cues: Wide stance, hands inside the knees
Open the hips, chest up, more upright torso
Push the floor apart with the feet
notes: Less spinal shear than conventional, more adductor and hip demand.

name: Trap Bar Deadlift
cues: Neutral grip, load in line with the body
More knee bend than a barbell deadlift
Stand up tall, don't hyperextend
notes: Cavaliere's substitution for anyone whose low back objects to conventional pulling. Better load position, lower shear, easier to learn.

name: Romanian Deadlift
cues: Push the hips back, soft knees held constant
Bar stays against the legs the whole way
Stop when the hamstrings stop, not when the floor arrives
notes: Best hip-dominant hamstring builder. The hamstring has two functions (hip extension, knee flexion) - program an RDL AND a leg curl, not one or the other.

name: Dumbbell Romanian Deadlift
cues: Dumbbells travel down the front of the legs
Hips back, chest proud
Feel the hamstring stretch, then reverse
notes: Easier to learn than the barbell RDL and each side loads independently. Grip typically fails before the hamstrings do.

name: Single-Leg Romanian Deadlift
cues: Hips stay square - don't let the free hip rotate open
Free leg extends straight back as a counterweight
Small range done well beats a big range done sloppily
notes: Cavaliere favourite for hip stability and asymmetry correction.

name: B-Stance Romanian Deadlift
cues: Back foot's toe lightly touching, heel up
~80% of the load on the front leg
Hips square, standard RDL hinge
notes: Most of the unilateral benefit with none of the balance limitation.

name: Good Morning
cues: Light load - much lighter than you expect
Hips back, spine rigid
Stop well short of a rounded back
notes: High spinal-erector cost. Cavaliere would substitute a back extension for most people.

name: Seated Good Morning
cues: Seated, bar on the back, hinge forward from the hips
Removes the balance and knee component
Light and controlled - this is spinal conditioning, not a max lift
notes: Ben Patrick's spinal/hamstring conditioning staple. Trains the hinge under load with the lower body fixed.

name: Lying Leg Curl
cues: Hips stay down on the pad
Full range - all the way down each rep
Point the toes to reduce calf involvement
notes: Knee-flexion hamstring function. Essential complement to RDLs.

name: Seated Leg Curl
cues: Hip flexed position puts the hamstring at a longer length
Thigh pad snug so the hips can't lift
Controlled 2-second eccentric
notes: Nippard rates the seated version above lying: the hip-flexed position lengthens the hamstring, and long-length training appears to grow it better.

name: Standing Single-Leg Curl
cues: Hips square against the pad
Curl the heel toward the glute
No hip extension to cheat
notes: Unilateral knee-flexion work. The most direct tool for correcting a side-to-side hamstring imbalance.

name: Nordic Hamstring Curl
cues: Ankles anchored, body straight from knees to head
Lower as slowly as you can, hips extended
Push off the hands to return if you can't pull yourself back
notes: The strongest evidence base of any Knees Over Toes movement - meaningful reduction in hamstring strain injury risk. Extremely soreness-inducing: start at 2 sets of 3 and build over weeks. ROM progression: measured as the lowest controlled descent point; full-range descent with an unassisted return is the terminal standard.

name: Eccentric-Only Nordic Curl
cues: Lower under control, catch yourself with the hands
Push back up with the arms - concentric doesn't count
3 sets of 5 is the classic ATG dose
notes: Standard middle rung of the Nordic ladder. ROM progression: measured as how far you descend under control before catching yourself on the hands.

name: Band-Assisted Nordic Curl
cues: Band anchored high behind you, looped under the chest
Reduce band tension as you get stronger
Body stays rigid - no hip hinge
notes: First rung of the Nordic ladder for most people. ROM progression: measured as the descent angle reached before the band takes the load; reduce band assistance as range improves.

name: Glute-Ham Raise
cues: Trains both hip extension and knee flexion in one rep
Push the toes into the plate
Keep the hips extended, don't pike
notes: Trains both hamstring functions simultaneously - rare and valuable.

name: 45-Degree Back Extension
cues: Round the upper back slightly to bias glutes/hams over erectors
Stop at body-line - do not hyperextend
Squeeze the glutes at the top
notes: Very high SFR posterior chain work with almost no systemic cost. Cavaliere's low-back-friendly substitute for good mornings.

name: Reverse Hyperextension
cues: Torso fixed, legs swing from the hips
No swinging momentum at the bottom
Stop the legs at body-line
notes: Traction plus posterior chain work. Popular in back-rehab-adjacent settings, though the decompression claims are not well established.

name: Barbell Hip Thrust
cues: Shoulder blades on the bench, chin tucked
Drive through the heels to full hip extension
Ribs down - extend at the hip, not the spine
notes: Highest-SFR glute movement. Peak tension in the shortened position, so pair with an RDL or deficit lunge for the stretch.

name: Single-Leg Hip Thrust
cues: Keep the hips level - no dropping on the free side
Full lockout, one-second squeeze
Ribs down throughout
notes: Unilateral glute work needing no barbell. Keeping the pelvis level through the whole rep is the actual exercise.

name: Barbell Glute Bridge
cues: Shoulders on the floor, shorter range than a hip thrust
Posterior tilt at the top
Heels close to the glutes
notes: Simpler setup than the hip thrust, shorter range.

name: Cable Pull-Through
cues: Face away from the stack, rope between the legs
Hips back, then snap to full extension
Spine neutral - the hips do all the work
notes: Best hinge-pattern teaching tool: the cable's line of pull tells you exactly where the hips should go. Near-zero spinal load.

name: Kettlebell Swing
cues: Hike the bell back between the legs
Snap the hips - the arms are just ropes
Bell floats to chest height, no higher
notes: Doubles as conditioning. Cavaliere's athletic hip-hinge power expression; Galpin-friendly as a low-eccentric conditioning modality.

name: Hip Adduction Machine
cues: Set a stretch-tolerable starting width
Squeeze the legs together, pause
Control the return into the stretch
notes: Underrated: adductor magnus is a large hip extensor and contributes real leg mass.

name: Hip Abduction Machine
cues: Lean forward slightly to bias glute medius
Push out and hold a beat
Slow return
notes: Glute medius work matters for knee tracking - Cavaliere programs abduction as knee-valgus prehab.

name: Copenhagen Plank
cues: Top leg on the bench, hold the body in a straight line
Start with the knee on the bench, progress to the foot
Prescribed in seconds
notes: Strongest evidence-based groin-strain prevention exercise. Time-based prescription.

name: Banded Lateral Walk
cues: Band above the knees or at the ankles
Small athletic stance, stay low
Push the knee out, don't let it cave
notes: Warm-up/activation, not a hypertrophy driver. Reps are steps per direction.

name: Standing Calf Raise
cues: Full stretch at the bottom, 2-second pause
Rise all the way onto the toes
No bouncing - the Achilles does all the work if you bounce
notes: Knee-straight position emphasises the gastrocnemius. Pause reps are the single biggest fix for stalled calves.

name: Seated Calf Raise
cues: Knee bent ~90 degrees isolates the soleus
Full range, pause at the bottom
Higher reps than standing
notes: Soleus is slow-twitch dominant and responds to higher reps. Program both seated and standing.

name: Single-Leg Calf Raise
cues: Off a step for full range
Balance with a fingertip on the wall
Same pause-at-the-bottom rule
notes: Reveals and fixes side-to-side asymmetry.

name: Leg Press Calf Raise
cues: Balls of the feet on the bottom of the platform
Safeties engaged before you start
Full stretch, full contraction
notes: Convenient calf loading inside a leg-press session. Engage the safeties before the first rep — this is a common way people get pinned.

name: Knees-Over-Toes Calf Raise
cues: Let the knee travel forward over the toes as you rise
Trains the calf and the knee's forward range together
Slow, full range, no bouncing
notes: Ben Patrick's calf variant: combines calf loading with the deep ankle dorsiflexion and knee-forward position the ATG system is built around. ROM progression: measured as forward knee travel past the toes while the heel stays loaded.

name: Tibialis Raise
cues: Back against a wall, heels ~12 inches out
Pull the toes up toward the shins as high as possible
Slow lower - the eccentric is the point
notes: First rung of the tibialis ladder. Ben Patrick's most-recommended entry movement: no equipment, high tolerance, 3 minutes.

name: Seated Tibialis Raise
cues: Band or weight over the forefoot, heel fixed
Full dorsiflexion each rep
Control the return
notes: Middle rung of the tibialis ladder: adds external load once wall tibialis raises have become easy.

name: Tib Bar Raise
cues: Bar hooked over the forefoot, heels planted
Pull the toes up to full dorsiflexion
Slow eccentric all the way down
notes: Loaded top of the tibialis ladder. Ben Patrick's published standard is 25% of bodyweight for 5 sets of 5. Descended from Bob Gajda's DARD device.

name: Hanging Leg Raise
cues: Posteriorly tilt the pelvis - curl the hips up, don't just lift the legs
No swinging between reps
Slow, controlled lowering
notes: Cavaliere's key point: if the pelvis doesn't tilt, it's a hip flexor exercise, not an ab exercise.

name: Hanging Knee Raise
cues: Knees to chest, tilting the pelvis at the top
Dead stop between reps
No momentum
notes: Entry point to hanging ab work. Progress to straight legs only once you can tilt the pelvis under control at the top.

name: Captain's Chair Knee Raise
cues: Back flat against the pad
Curl the pelvis up at the top
Lower slowly
notes: Removes the grip limitation of hanging variations.

name: Reverse Crunch
cues: Lift the hips off the floor, not just the knees
Low back stays pressed down
Slow eccentric
notes: Best entry point for lower-ab-biased work.

name: Cable Crunch
cues: Hips stay fixed - flex the spine, don't hinge
Crunch the ribcage toward the pelvis
Resist on the way up
notes: The only common ab movement that loads spinal flexion progressively. Best hypertrophy option for the rectus abdominis.

name: Crunch
cues: Curl the ribs toward the pelvis
Hands light at the head - don't pull the neck
Short controlled range
notes: Unloaded spinal flexion. Fine as a starting point, but it has no real progression path — graduate to cable crunches once you can do 25.

name: Ab Wheel Rollout
cues: Posteriorly tilt the pelvis before you roll
Only roll as far as you can keep the low back from arching
Ribs down the whole way
notes: Anti-extension work. Rolling out further than you can control is the classic way people hurt their back on this. ROM progression: measured as rollout distance (or ramp/incline angle) at which the lumbar spine still holds neutral.

name: Plank
cues: Elbows under shoulders, glutes squeezed
Posterior pelvic tilt - hips slightly tucked
Prescribed in seconds; if you can hold 2 minutes, progress instead of adding time
notes: Time-based. Cavaliere's view: long static planks have diminishing returns - progress to loaded or dynamic anti-extension work.

name: Side Plank
cues: Stack the feet, hips high
Straight line ear to ankle
Time-based, both sides
notes: Time-based.

name: Pallof Press
cues: Stand perpendicular to the cable, press straight out
Resist the rotation - nothing should turn
Hold at full extension for 2 seconds
notes: Cavaliere staple: the core's real job is resisting motion, not creating it.

name: Cable Woodchop
cues: Rotate from the hips and mid-back, not the low back
Pivot the back foot
Control the return
notes: Rotational power. Cavaliere's 'train like an athlete' plane-of-motion coverage.

name: Dead Bug
cues: Low back pressed into the floor the whole time
Extend opposite arm and leg slowly
Exhale as you extend
notes: Safest entry point for anyone with a sensitive low back.

name: Bird Dog
cues: Hips and shoulders stay square to the floor
Reach long, don't lift high
Pause 2 seconds at full extension
notes: Anti-rotation plus spinal endurance.

name: L-Sit
cues: Push the shoulders down away from the ears
Legs straight and together, toes pointed
Time-based hold
notes: Time-based. High skill.

name: Russian Twist
cues: Rotate from the mid-back, not by flinging the arms
Chest tall, don't collapse
Slow and deliberate
notes: Loaded lumbar rotation under fatigue is a questionable risk/reward. Prefer Pallof presses and chops. Included for completeness.

name: Neck Harness Extension
cues: Very light load to start - the neck is not the low back
Slow, full range, no jerking
Stop at any dizziness or tingling
notes: Athlete/contact-sport population. Progress load extremely slowly.

name: Plate Neck Flexion
cues: Lie face up, plate on a towel over the forehead
Chin tuck, then curl the head up
Very light, very slow
notes: Anterior neck loading. Very light and very slow: the neck responds well to small doses and punishes large jumps.

name: Neck Isometric Hold
cues: Hand or band provides resistance, head doesn't move
Build pressure gradually over 3 seconds
All four directions, time-based
notes: Safest neck entry point. Time-based.

name: Cable External Rotation
cues: Elbow at 90 degrees, tucked at the side (or on a pad at 90 abduction)
Rotate the forearm outward, upper arm stays put
Very light - 2-8 kg is a working weight
notes: Direct infraspinatus/teres minor work. Cavaliere prescribes 2x/week for anyone doing meaningful pressing volume.

name: Side-Lying External Rotation
cues: Lie on your side, towel under the elbow
Elbow glued to the ribs, rotate the forearm up
Tiny weight - this is not a strength lift
notes: Entry-level rotator cuff work, no equipment beyond a light dumbbell.

name: Wall Slide
cues: Forearms on the wall, ribs down
Slide up while keeping contact
Reach at the top - let the shoulder blades rotate upward
notes: Serratus and lower trap activation. Best pre-press warm-up in the library.

name: Quadruped Thoracic Rotation
cues: Hand behind the head, rotate the elbow to the ceiling
Rotation comes from the mid-back, hips stay square
Exhale at end range
notes: Thoracic rotation. Poor T-spine rotation forces the shoulder and low back to compensate.

name: Thoracic Extension over Foam Roller
cues: Roller across the mid-back, hands supporting the head
Extend over the roller, exhale
Move the roller up one segment at a time
notes: Prep for overhead pressing and front-rack positions.

name: Couch Stretch
aliases: rear foot elevated hip flexor stretch
cues: Back foot up the wall, front foot planted
Squeeze the glute of the back leg to protect the low back
Time-based, breathe through it
notes: KOT hip mobility staple. The glute squeeze is what makes it a hip flexor stretch rather than a lumbar extension. Time-based. ROM progression: measured as torso angle — advance from hands-down toward a fully upright torso with the pelvis posteriorly tilted.

name: Half-Kneeling Hip Flexor Stretch
cues: Posteriorly tilt the pelvis first, then lean
Ribs down
Time-based
notes: Regression of the couch stretch. Time-based.

name: 90/90 Hip Switch
cues: Both knees at 90 degrees, switch sides without using hands
Chest tall
Slow and controlled - this is strength through range, not a stretch
notes: Internal and external hip rotation. Reps = switches per side.

name: Elephant Walk
cues: Hands on the floor, alternate straightening each leg
Keep the hands down as the knees alternate
Reps = alternations
notes: Ben Patrick's hamstring/calf mobility staple. Precursor to the Jefferson curl. ROM progression: measured as knee extension achieved while the palms stay flat on the floor.

name: Jefferson Curl
cues: Stand on a box, roll down one vertebra at a time
Very light load - 5-10 kg is a serious working weight
Never rush; never load this heavy
notes: Deliberate loaded spinal flexion, and the most contested movement in this library. Ben Patrick programs it for spinal resilience; that is a coach-specific position, not a settled one, and the supporting evidence is thin. Rules if you use it: start completely unloaded and stay unloaded for weeks; a 5-10 kg working weight is already serious; never near failure; never rushed. Contraindicated for anyone with current or historical disc symptoms, radiating leg pain, or any back pain at rest — those users should skip it entirely and speak to a clinician. Not included in any default program template; it appears only if a user seeks it out. ROM progression: measured as depth below the box at which the spine still segments smoothly under a light load.

name: Ankle Dorsiflexion Mobilization
cues: Drive the knee over the toes, heel stays down
Foot 4-5 inches from the wall to start
Reps = rocks per side
notes: Prerequisite for deep squatting and the ATG split squat. ROM progression: measured as knee-to-wall distance in centimetres with the heel staying down.

name: Deep Squat Hold
cues: Sit in the bottom of a full squat, heels down
Elbows inside the knees, push them out
Time-based - accumulate minutes daily
notes: Time-based. KOT baseline position: if you can't sit here comfortably, that's the first thing to fix. ROM progression: measured as heel-down squat depth and torso angle; a flat-footed, upright, full-depth squat is the standard.

name: Backward Sled Drag
cues: Walk backward, pulling the sled with straps or handles
Stay low, knees bending and travelling forward
Prescribed in metres or seconds - typically 2 x 50 yards
notes: Ben Patrick calls this the #1 exercise for longevity: concentric-only quad loading, so it builds knee strength and conditioning with almost no soreness and no eccentric damage. Published benchmark ~50% bodyweight. Also an ideal low-eccentric conditioning modality by Galpin's criteria.

name: Forward Sled Push
cues: Low body angle, arms locked out
Short powerful steps
Distance- or time-based, not reps
notes: Concentric-only, so it produces conditioning stimulus with minimal recovery cost. Excellent same-day pairing with lifting.

name: Backward Treadmill Walk
cues: Slow speed, hold the rails at first
Let the knees travel forward with each step
Prescribed in seconds
notes: The no-sled substitute for backward sled work. Time-based.

name: Zone 2 Cycling
cues: 60-75% max HR - you can hold a conversation
Steady cadence, no surges
Prescribed in seconds of duration
notes: Best Zone 2 modality for lifters: no eccentric loading, so it doesn't compete with leg hypertrophy. Galpin's target is 150-180 min/week of Zone 2 total. Duration in seconds.

name: Zone 2 Incline Walk
cues: 8-12% incline, 4-5 km/h
Don't hold the rails - it invalidates the effort
Talk test: conversational but effortful
notes: Lowest-skill Zone 2 option, near-zero interference with lifting. Duration in seconds.

name: Zone 2 Rowing
cues: Legs, then hips, then arms - in that order
20-24 strokes per minute for Zone 2
Duration in seconds
notes: Full-body Zone 2. Slightly more upper-back fatigue than cycling - account for it if pull volume is already high.

name: Zone 2 Swimming
cues: Conversational effort between intervals
Zero impact - best option with lower-limb pain
Duration in seconds
notes: Zero eccentric load. HR runs ~10 bpm lower in water - adjust zone targets accordingly.

name: Zone 2 Stair Climber
cues: Steady pace, upright posture
Don't lean on the handles
Duration in seconds
notes: Higher glute/quad demand than walking - counts against lower-body recovery budget.

name: Rucking
cues: 10-20% bodyweight in a pack, weight high on the back
Brisk pace, upright posture
Duration in seconds
notes: Zone 2 plus postural/grip endurance. Start light - rucking soreness sneaks up on people.

name: VO2max Intervals (Run)
cues: 4 minutes at 90-95% max HR, 3 minutes easy, x4
You should not be able to talk during the work interval
Rep range = seconds per work interval
notes: Gold-standard VO2max protocol. Highest-eccentric conditioning option - if leg hypertrophy is the goal, use the bike or rower version instead. First thing cut when readiness is low.

name: Air Bike Intervals
cues: Full effort on the work interval, easy spin between
Common formats: 4x4 min, or 10x30 s all-out
Rep range = seconds per work interval
notes: Best high-intensity option for lifters: zero eccentric loading, brutal cardiovascular stimulus.

name: Rowing Intervals
cues: Drive with the legs, hold a consistent split
500 m repeats or 4x4 min work intervals
Rep range = seconds per work interval
notes: Full-body intervals with no eccentric loading. A good VO2max option when running would interfere with leg training.

name: Sprint Intervals
cues: Warm up thoroughly - cold sprinting is how hamstrings tear
Full recovery between reps (2-4 min)
Rep range = seconds per sprint
notes: Highest hamstring-strain risk in the library. Requires a real warm-up and build-up; never program for a deconditioned user. Pair with Nordic curls.

name: Jump Rope
cues: Small hops, stay on the balls of the feet
Wrists turn the rope, not the arms
Duration in seconds
notes: Calf and foot conditioning plus Zone 2-3 work. High cumulative Achilles load - build volume gradually.

name: Box Jump
cues: Land softly, knees tracking over the toes
Step down, never jump down
Low reps, full recovery - this is a power exercise, not conditioning
notes: Never program to fatigue. Cavaliere's rule: box jumps are about landing mechanics, and box height is ego, not training.

name: Depth Drop
cues: Step off a low box, absorb the landing
Land quietly - noise means poor absorption
Start at 12 inches and progress slowly over months
notes: Eccentric landing capacity. High tissue stress - only for people with a solid strength base.

name: Broad Jump
cues: Arms swing back then drive forward
Full triple extension
Stick the landing before measuring the distance
notes: Horizontal power. Ben Patrick's standards use broad jump as an athleticism benchmark.

name: Pogo Hops
cues: Minimal knee bend - bounce from the ankles
Stay tall, short ground contacts
Think 'hot floor'
notes: Achilles stiffness and reactive strength. Best entry point into plyometrics.

name: Skater Bound
cues: Push off laterally, land on the opposite leg
Stick each landing before the next bound
Knee tracks over the toe, doesn't cave in
notes: Frontal-plane power and knee-valgus control.

name: Medicine Ball Slam
cues: Full overhead reach, then drive the ball down
Hips and abs do the work, not the arms
Catch or reset - don't chase the bounce
notes: Explosive trunk flexion, doubles as conditioning.

name: Medicine Ball Rotational Throw
cues: Pivot the back foot, rotate through the hips
Throw hard - intent is the stimulus
Both sides equally
notes: Rotational power. Cavaliere's athletic-quality core work.

name: Tuck Jump
cues: Jump, tuck the knees, land soft
Reset between reps
Stop the set the moment landings get sloppy
notes: Repeated hard landings - high knee stress. Never program to fatigue.
